newsitem.title: USA: Smoking quadruples breast cancer risk in many women.
newsitem.headline: Smoking quadruples breast cancer risk in many women.

text.p: Smoking quadruples an older woman's risk of contracting breast cancer if she is among those with a slow-acting form of an enzyme that detoxifies the carcinogens in cigarette smoke, a study said Tuesday.

The risk of breast cancer in postmenopausal women who have the slow form of the enzyme, N-acetyltransferase 2, increased depending on how much they smoked and whether they smoked when young but was not related to the duration of their habit.
Neither the enzyme form nor smoking alone was independently associated with breast cancer risk, the study, in the Journal of the American Medical Association, said.

An estimated 55 percent of white postmenopausal American women have the slower form of the enzyme, while up to 90 percent of women of Middle Eastern descent have it. African American and Asian women are less likely to have it. The enzyme is believed to help the body detoxify tobacco-related carcinogens.

Women who smoked at or before age 16 and adult women who were heavier smokers and have the slow-acting enzyme had four times the risk of developing breast cancer after the onset of menopause than those who had never smoked, the study found.

"Our data suggest that, for more than half the white female population of the United States, avoidance of breast cancer may be yet another motivation for avoiding cigarette smoking, particularly at an early age," study author Christine Ambrosone of the National Center for Toxicological Research in Jefferson, Arkansas, wrote.
